nodes.text: Let $r\geq 2$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ be such that $A_i\not\subseteq A_j$ for all $i\neq j$ and for any $t$ if there exists some $i$ with $\lvert A_i\rvert=t$ then there must exist at least $r$ sets of that size. How large must $n$ be (as a function of $r$) to ensure that there is such a family which achieves $n-3$ distinct sizes of sets?

#776 : [Er81i] [Gu83] combinatorics A problem of Erdős and Trotter. For $r=1$ and $n>3$ the maximum possible is $n-2$. For $r>1$ and $n$ sufficiently large $n-3$ is achievable, but $n-2$ is never achievable. Let $n_0(r)$ be such that whenever $n>n_0(r)$ there exists such a family with $n-3$ distinct set sizes. He and Tang [HeTa26b] (with ChatGPT) have proved that $n_0(2)=3$, $n_0(3)=8$, and for all $r\geq 4$\[2r+2\leq n_0(r)\leq 2r+2\log_2r+O(\log\log r),\]and hence $n_0(r)\sim 2r$ as $r\to \infty$.
